articles.title: Fire on passenger ferry in Philippines leaves dozens missing and at least 5 dead
articles.summary: The ferry MV June Aster had sailed from Manila and was near Coron in Palawan province when the fire started Wednesday.
articles.body: MANILA, Philippines — A fire broke out on a passenger ferry off the western Philippines, leaving dozens of people missing, the coast guard said Thursday. At least five people were killed. So far, 42 people have been rescued and efforts are ongoing, so the count of 87 people missing may change, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said in a radio interview. The ferry MV June Aster had sailed from Manila and was near Coron in Palawan province when the fire started around 6:45 p.m. (6:45 a.m. ET) Wednesday. Images from the scene showed the ferry was still on fire. Coast guard personnel tossed life jackets to survivors as the ferry burned in the background. Passengers were helped into smaller boats taking them to shallow water, and body bags were laid out at what looked like a port. Bad weather and big waves were challenging rescuers. The ferry was around 4 nautical miles off Coron’s village of Turda when it sent a distress signal, but strong sea currents had dragged it to a distance of 7.68 nautical miles off Turda. She said 134 people were on board, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. “Based on the data that we have right now, the rescued and casualty, we are still searching for 87 people,” she told DZXL radio. There was no information about any foreigners on board, coast guard information officer Joy Gumatay told reporters. Cayabyab said it was still unclear what caused the fire, and that the coast guard was coordinating with the shipping company and maritime authorities to get more details. Ferries are a common transportation method in the Philippine archipelago. Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces. In 1987, the ferry Doña Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world’s deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

images.caption: In this image provided by the Philippine Coast Guard, a survivor is assisted as he alights from a small boat after being rescued from a burning ferry off Palawan province, Philippines on Wednesday Sept. 9, 2026.

articles.title: Exclusive: This small island off Yemen is now a strategic prize in the widening Iran war
articles.summary: Perim Island sits in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a pinch-point that’s taken on outsized importance since the war with Iran effectively shuttered the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body: Stepping on to the Yemeni island of Perim is to relive history. Its barren sand and rock moonscape feels for all the world like the land that time forgot. Its location, however, has put it at the heart of a very modern conflict. For Perim Island sits in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, a geopolitical pinch-point that’s taken on an outsized importance since US President Donald Trump’s war with Iran effectively shuttered the Strait of Hormuz. To help keep global energy supplies flowing, and prices down, Saudi Arabia diverted its oil exports from Hormuz to the Red Sea. But now Yemen’s Houthi rebels, Iran’s most powerful regional proxy, have begun an offensive that could land them control of Perim – and with it the ability to prevent ships passing through this narrow gateway from the Red Sea. Regional sources told CNN Thursday that the Houthis were making major push to capture the town of Mocha, a crucial coastal location some 50 miles to the north of Perim. On a recent day, an honor guard of Yemeni troops, patiently shuffling in the scorching sun, watched while a weathered officer’s outstretched hand helped arrivals to Perim off an aging gunboat. A CNN crew was among them, granted exclusive access to this dusty outpost. The tableau, reminiscent of a bygone era, has likely played out here for centuries. The island’s position – at the narrowest point of a strait which brings the Horn of Africa within 12 miles of the Arabian Peninsula – has made it valuable to empires and regional powers for generations. Once a coaling station for ships of the British Empire sailing to India, Perim’s imperial past is still visible in its crumbling ruins. Bumping along a rocky road to the island’s highest point, the officer – one hand on the wheel of his decrepit army truck – points to Eritrea and Djibouti across the water, on the African side of the strait. A veteran member of a brigade loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government, he knows his mission, defending Perim, also known as Mayyun, now carries far greater stakes than before. ‘It’s geopolitical now’ For more than a decade, Yemen’s civil war appeared to be a distant regional conflict. But as fighting intensifies and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launch attacks towards the Red Sea coast, that distinction is disappearing. Yemen, with Perim at the center, is becoming another potential front line in the confrontation between Washington and Tehran, and a reminder that the consequences of its war no longer stop at its shores. Already, the Houthis control Yemen’s capital, swaths of the country’s northwest, and much of its Red Sea coastline north of the island. If history is any guide, Bab al-Mandab – the smaller twin of the Strait of Hormuz and now a crucial alternative to it – could be where Iran, through its proxy, tightens the economic and political screws on Trump next, driving up oil prices and damaging Republican prospects in the US midterm elections in November. “We told the world that this is an Iranian project, but no one listened to Yemenis back then… It’s geopolitical now,” Tarik Saleh, a vice president in Yemen’s beleaguered, internationally recognized government, told CNN in an exclusive interview. Saleh, a nephew of the ousted president Ali Abdullah Saleh and a former ally of the Houthis, is a rarity among Yemen’s political class: the only leader and military commander who remains inside the country while many others have fled. He says he has survived several assassination attempts and says Iran wants him dead. Meetings with him are arranged at short notice, in random locations, and are over fast. Speaking to CNN from a tent on a remote Yemeni beach in late August, Saleh said he was receiving no help from the United States, “only talk.” He warned that if the Houthis seized Perim Island and gained control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, “then a massive (international) force and the navies will be needed” to dislodge them. Even reaching Perim Island is a lesson in the dangers of this often one-sidedly high-tech war. As the CNN team set out for the two-mile crossing from the mainland, warnings of an imminent Houthi drone attack forced the gunboat carrying the crew to turn back. Preparing for a possible attack, the gunner fired a heavy-caliber round from his rusting weapon. ‘In bed together’ Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, and drove the internationally recognized government into exile. Saudi Arabia led a military campaign the following year to dislodge the rebels. Iran has supplied the Houthis with weapons and training, and exercises some influence on the rebel group’s decisions. The result is a fractured country, with the Houthis controlling the capital and the northwest, and the government and allied factions holding much of the south and east. Some 22 million people, roughly half of the population, need humanitarian assistance to this day. Following the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel and the ensuing war on Gaza, the Houthis joined the conflict. They launched attacks on Israel in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and targeted shipping in the Red Sea. The US and Israel launched airstrikes on the group that destroyed key assets. The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a terror group in 2025. The latest Houthi offensive against Yemen’s government began in July. It ruptured a tacit four-year truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia and drew Yemen’s conflict into the wider war involving Iran. In a rare exception to restrictions it has enforced over Yemeni airspace since intervening in 2015, Saudi Arabia permitted an Iranian passenger plane to land in Sanaa. The plane – the first direct air link between Tehran and Sanaa in about a decade – then carried a Houthi delegation to the funeral of Ali Khamenei, Iran’s former supreme leader, who was killed alongside several members of his family in the opening US-Israeli strikes of February 28. But when the aircraft returned 10 days later, Saudi Arabia denied it permission to land in Sanaa amid concerns that it was also carrying Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel and military equipment. Saudi aircraft struck the airport’s runway, forcing the plane to divert to the Houthi-controlled Yemeni port city of Hodeidah. The episode became a turning point, unraveling diplomacy that had largely preserved the informal truce and halted Houthi attacks on Saudi territory. Against the backdrop of the collapsing US-Iran ceasefire, the Houthis retaliated by declaring a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and threatening ships carrying Saudi exports through Bab al-Mandab. They also launched missiles and drones at the kingdom’s oil infrastructure, airports and other civilian sites. The timing of the new Houthi offensive could benefit Iran by increasing pressure on Trump. Mohammed Al-Basha, a former Yemeni government press officer and Washington, DC-based risk analyst, described the relationship between Tehran and the Houthis as “not a submissive relationship – but they are in bed together.” Nonetheless, observers caution against framing the Houthis’ recent intervention as merely executing Iran’s regional agenda. “The Houthis needed a war as diversion from domestic problems. They wanted to say they can fight Saudi Arabia into negotiating with them again. And of course, if it is going to help an old friend, like Iran, which at one point was the only friend they had, then why not?” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Chatham House think tank research fellow. The Houthi attacks on Israel, and the weakening of other Iranian allies in the region like Hezbollah in Lebanon, as well as the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, have elevated the Yemeni faction’s standing in the so-called axis of resistance and the Houthis wanted to capitalize on their new position, he added. Sanaa officials have not responded to CNN’s request for comment. Houthi leaders have maintained in previous statements that their current offensive inside and outside Yemen is in response to “Saudi aggression and blockade.” Strikes on port, fishermen Oil flows past Perim have already fallen sharply amid this maritime roulette. Three years ago, about 10% of the world’s seaborne oil trade passed through Bab al-Mandab. Kpler data indicates that volume has since fallen by half, and a sustained Houthi campaign could choke the route further. Yemen’s fishermen are also victims of Houthi drone attacks. Dozens were evacuated from an island north of Perim after one such attack killed and injured several people, according to Yemeni government officials. As fishermen wrestled their catches out of flimsy fiberglass boats near a makeshift shoreside market recently, several stopped to talk with CNN, complaining that the war is ruining business. On normal days, one trader said, “there would be many ships out there,” but “because of the attack of the Houthi there are no ships right now.” Children played in the Red Sea’s lukewarm waves. Apparently unconcerned about their parents’ worries, they jostled to get into the visiting journalists’ pictures. But the image that emerges here is of an already war-weary, fragile and poor country being pushed ever closer to a breaking point. A few miles up the coast, evidence of that is mounting. The port of Mocha, the most northerly government-held city of significance on the Red Sea, is being hit hard. A few weeks ago, more than 25 Houthi rockets slammed into the sprawling harbor as commercial ships were unloading, according to port director Abdel Malek Al-Sharaabi. In the water, half-sunk ships lie at improbable angles, while the concrete on land is scarred with holes deep enough to hide a large dog. Heaps of scorched motorcycle frames lie beside piles of semi-melted engines. Sixteen people were killed and 22 injured that day, the port director told CNN, while six commercial ships were sunk and 14,000 motorcycles lost. The Houthis, he said, want to destroy the economy. “The port had a big role in development and commerce,” Al-Sharaabi said. “This attack aims at hurting this development and stopping services.” Over the past year, the Houthis have repeatedly fired at targets as far as Israel, more than 1,000 miles away. They claim to possess hypersonic missiles and have an arsenal that includes long-range, sea-skimming anti-ship missiles designed to evade radar. They also possess surface-to-air missiles capable of downing high-altitude US drones and threatening crewed aircraft. ‘Higher price in the future’ On Yemen’s front lines, fighting between Houthi and government forces is intensifying. Government troops are flying new, first-person-view, or FPV, quadcopter drones, attacking concealed Houthi bunkers. “Our troops have improved due to training and new resources like drones,” Saleh told CNN. But for every step the government takes, officials say, Iran is trying to keep the Houthis ahead. A journey in a vehicle with blacked-out windows to a heavily guarded warehouse at a secret location offered a glimpse of that challenge – and what the government says is evidence of the scale of Iranian support for the Houthis, including the provision of weapons capable of threatening tanker traffic in the Red Sea. Abdel Nasser El Mamlouh, the director of Saleh’s military media operation, led CNN through what he said was an Iranian-made weapons shipment captured before smugglers could deliver it to the Houthis. The cache included enormous, 18-foot-long missiles, complex long-range radar systems, drone engines and optical equipment, even bullets hidden inside a truck battery. Everything, El Mamlouh said, had been disguised as commercial equipment to evade detection. And what they captured, he readily acknowledged, was only a fraction of what is believed to have made it through. Smugglers “confessed that before this one they had smuggled 11 shipments similar in size and content,” he said, amounting to 750 tons. If the Houthis seized Perim and gained a foothold in Bab al-Mandab, he warned, they would no longer need long-range weapons to threaten shipping. “They would mine the strait, just like (Iran) did in Hormuz,” he said. Along Yemen’s government-held stretch of Red Sea coast, officials have little doubt that their civil war has become part of something much larger. “(We are) fighting this war on behalf of the Arab world and the international community,” Mamlouh said. Before hurrying away from his tent on the beach, Saleh was asked what would happen if US support never came. “We will pay a higher price in the future,” to dislodge the Houthis, he replied. And so, he warned, would “the American army, the international community and international trade.” CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany contributed to this report.

articles.title: Funeral for PC Clough killed in Middlesbrough A66 crash
articles.summary: PC Tom Clough's family say they are grateful for the public's support.
articles.body:
The funeral for the second police officer killed in a wrong-way crash while on duty will take place later on Thursday.

PC Tom Clough, 38, died on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of 22 August alongside his colleague PC Matthew Blades when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed police car. The five young men in the Passat also died.

Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said PC Clough's partner had said public support "brought them so much strength".

Officers had been pursuing the Passat seconds before it collided with PC Blades and PC Clough's car on the dual carriageway.

The pair had been looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, according to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The Passat's occupants - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17 - also died.

PC Clough had served in the Army and Somerville said she had "the privilege" of speaking to his partner.

"The family are grateful for all of the support from the public, it's brought them so much strength," Somerville said.

"She wants people to know that Tom wasn't just a police officer, he was a partner and a brother and a son and most importantly a father to a sausage dog called Frank, who was the love of his life."

More than £1.2m was raised to help the families of PC Blades and PC Clough , a fundraiser which was set up by Cleveland Police Federation.

"Tom used to say that he didn't think anybody would come to his funeral and he was wrong," Somerville said.

"He was described as giving his everything to everybody."

articles.title: A car crash left this Army veteran paralysed; seven years later, he graduated with a petroleum engineering degree
articles.summary: US News: Rocky Fernandez’s life took an unexpected turn when a car crash left the Army veteran paralysed, forcing him to rebuild plans that had once seemed str.
articles.body: Rocky Fernandez’s life took an unexpected turn when a car crash left the Army veteran paralysed, forcing him to rebuild plans that had once seemed straightforward. Recovery brought hospital stays, rehabilitation and medical setbacks, but his ambitions did not disappear. As reported by the US Department of Veterans Affairs, with support from the Houston VA and vocational services, Fernandez returned to education and worked towards a petroleum engineering degree. Seven years after the accident, he reached a milestone that once seemed difficult to imagine: graduation. His journey involved far more than completing coursework, requiring him to balance ongoing health challenges with college and daily life. Now, he is preparing to begin a career in petroleum engineering.Rocky Fernandez’s life changed after a car crash left him paralysedBefore the crash, Fernandez was an Army veteran with plans that centred on education and what might come afterwards. The accident altered those plans almost immediately.The years that followed were marked by medical complications and rehabilitation. There were extended periods in hospital, including treatment for a serious infection, while adapting to life with paralysis brought a different set of demands outside the hospital as well.Going back to college was therefore not simply a matter of returning to a classroom. Fernandez had to work around circumstances that could make attending classes, studying and managing everyday tasks considerably more complicated.Reportedly, he found support at the Michael E. DeBakey VA Medical Center in Houston, where treatment was accompanied by services aimed at helping him regain some independence and continue pursuing his education.VA support helped Fernandez stay focused on collegeVocational support became an important part of that process. Shaun Smith, Fernandez’s vocational counsellor at the VA, helped him work through some of the obstacles between his circumstances and his college plans.For Fernandez, that assistance formed part of a much larger effort. Medical care, rehabilitation and practical support all had to fit around the same goal: getting his education finished.His vocational counselor Shaun Smith said Fernandez's approach was striking because he remained focused on what he wanted to achieve rather than allowing each setback to change the destination.“I’m not gonna lie, it was hard to have faith after all these setbacks,” Fernandez said. He eventually learned to slow things down, deal with what was in front of him and keep moving.His recovery extended beyond medical treatmentFernandez has also become a regular presence at the Houston VA's wellness programmes. Among the activities he attends is weekly yoga, where he works with yoga therapist Darcy Robinson.His sessions have included meditation, deep relaxation and sound-bowl therapy alongside yoga. Robinson described Fernandez as willing to experiment with different approaches to his wellbeing, rather than treating rehabilitation as something confined to conventional medical appointments.For staff who have worked with Fernandez, these activities have offered another view of his recovery. He is not only someone receiving care. He has also become familiar to people around the medical centre, where his regular presence and interactions with staff have made him a recognisable figure.Fernandez’s recovery has also inspired him to help other veteransDr Donna Huang, one of the physicians involved in his care, said Fernandez continued to think about other veterans even while dealing with his own complicated medical course. During the early stages of rehabilitation, he was already considering how he might eventually support people facing spinal cord injuries themselves.Fernandez came to view disability as part of the range of human experience rather than something that should determine what a person can or cannot attempt. He hoped to become a peer support partner for veterans dealing with similar injuries.Huang said, “What stood out about taking care of Rocky was his unwavering resilience and optimism in the face of a complicated medical course with multiple setbacks.”Fernandez now puts that idea into simpler terms. He believes there are fewer fixed boundaries around what a person can accomplish than circumstances might initially suggest.After years of setbacks, Fernandez finally earned his degreeThe graduation this spring marked the completion of a course of study that began before his accident and continued through years of profound change.Fernandez now has a petroleum engineering degree from Houston City College. The qualification does not erase the medical complications or the limitations he still lives with. It does, however, give him something concrete to build on after a period in which much of his life had to be reorganised around recovery.His next step is already taking shape. He is looking for work in petroleum engineering and wants to use the degree he worked so long to obtain.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Dartford Larder social supermarket reports hundreds of sign-ups
articles.summary: Dartford Larder members pay £4.50 each week for items including unlimited fruit and vegetables.
articles.body:
A "social supermarket" offering low cost groceries and budgeting advice says it has had 600 sign-ups in its first year.

The Dartford Larder in Kent opened in July 2025 and operates a subscription model, where members pay £4.50 to visit each week for essential items including unlimited fruit and vegetables.

The facility, on Copperfields Walk, is run by Crossways Community Church, the Healthy Living Centre and Dartford Borough Council.

The church's pastor, Stephen Brindley, said organisers had "achieved what we intended to with the project, which was giving people back dignity".

He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that users had welcomed the subscription system as they felt they were "giving something in return for what they were getting".

He said: "When we were a food bank, there were many people who would not come through the door because of the stigma which was attached.

"The supermarket takes a lot of that away because, at the end of the day, it looks and operates as a normal supermarket."

More than 75,000 items have been distributed since the Dartford Larder opened, according to the pastor.

He added: "We're just doing it from our heart and our passion and I think it's had a really, really good impact."

articles.title: AI is taking my work, says graphic designer
articles.summary: Danny Williams says small businesses are increasingly turning to AI to generate posters.
articles.body:
A graphic designer has said he is losing business due to smaller firms choosing to generate their own content using artificial intelligence (AI).

Danny Williams, from East Yorkshire, said he understood why companies, in tough economic times, would choose to go down the AI path.

He added: "With smaller businesses, the funding isn't there for graphic design or big media packs."

Stephen Woodford, CEO of the Advertising Association, said the industry was seeing "rapid change" through the adoption of AI, but said strict rules need to be adhered to.

Graphic designers were "in demand" 15 years ago when he started out, according to Williams, who added: "I'm getting less work now, to be honest."

Williams said AI was becoming "more and more accessible" and accepted the graphic design sector needed to "adapt", but he claimed posters generated using the latest methods were becoming repetitive.

"Most people are sick of seeing them," he said.

He added: "At the end of the day, it's the face of your business.

"I do believe it will come full circle again because people are literally sick of seeing AI and they don't trust AI."

Claire Howlett, landlady of The King's Head pub in Pollington, East Yorkshire, said she uses AI to make the majority of her social media content.

She said: "I've done all my advertising myself so far. Maybe in the future, if the business got bigger, I might use a graphic designer, but I'm finding the AI tools available to us are fit for purpose at the moment.

"As far as I'm concerned, you want the best option, the cheapest option and the most convenient, which is AI at the moment."

Woodford said the Advertising Association's goal was to ensure the UK advertising industry "harnesses the efficiencies of AI while maintaining the high creative standards, public trust, and ethical safeguards".

He said AI was "enormously capable", but added "there are things it cannot do".

Advertising is a heavily regulated industry, said Woodford, with distributed material needing to be "decent, honest and truthful".

"If you're putting things in the public domain on behalf of a brand or a business, you've got to be absolutely sure that they are representing that business honestly and with integrity and in compliance with the rules," he added.

articles.title: Fighting escalates in Yemen; Houthi attacks trigger alerts in Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Yemen’s government accuses Houthis of killing three children as rebels claim Saudi forces launched 54 air raids in 12 hours.
articles.body:
Fighting has escalated across Yemen, with the country’s internationally recognised government blaming the Houthis for an artillery attack that killed three children, while Saudi Arabia accused the Iran-backed group of continuing to strike the kingdom’s infrastructure.

The claims on Wednesday came as the Houthis promised to retaliate for what they said were 54 Saudi airstrikes in a 12-hour span.

The renewed hostilities between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis are unfolding amid intensifying regional tensions set off by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. Pakistan warned on Tuesday that continued Houthi attacks could trigger the recently signed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a mutual security pact involving Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.

According to the World Health Organization, the clashes have killed or wounded more than 1,000 people and displaced tens of thousands.

On Wednesday, the government-run Saba news reported that at least three children, including a baby, were killed in Houthi shelling in the central Marib governorate. Six others were also wounded in the attack, which Saba said was the second of its kind in 48 hours.

The first assault killed two children and wounded 15 others, it said.

The Houthis did not comment on the claim, but said the death toll from what it said was a Saudi attack on a prison in the northern al-Jawf governorate on Tuesday had climbed to at least 32 people. Some seven others were wounded, the group said.

Yemen has been mired in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The attack prompted a Saudi-led military intervention the following year and a devastating conflict that killed an estimated 150,000 people.

A United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 brought a halt to large-scale fighting, but clashes resumed again in July following a strike by government forces on the Houthi-held Sanaa airport. The Houthis last week launched a major offensive in Hodeidah and Taiz provinces aimed at advancing towards the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical maritime waterway for Saudi oil exports.

That offensive prompted government-aligned forces to mount counterattacks and expand operations elsewhere in the country, including in the al-Jawf governorate, considered a gateway to Sanaa.

The fighting has continued to spill over into Saudi Arabia.

A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, Major General Turki al-Maliki, said on Wednesday the Houthis were “persisting” in attacks on the kingdom’s assets and infrastructure, adding that the rebels had targeted Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan using ballistic missiles and drones.

He promised that the coalition would respond to what he called the Houthis’ “heinous attacks”.

Saudi Arabia’s civil defence authority also issued multiple alerts for Khamis Mushait and Abha on Wednesday and early on Thursday.

No casualties were reported in connection with those alerts.

Earlier, a Houthi military spokesman said Saudi forces had launched 54 air strikes across six provinces over 12 hours on Wednesday, targeting al-Jawf, Marib, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada and al-Bayda. Yahya Saree did not say whether the attacks had caused casualties, but said the aircraft involved had taken off from King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and King Fahd Air Base in Taif.

“These air strikes and the ongoing aggression against our country will not go unanswered and unpunished, by the will and power of God,” Saree said.

The Houthis had on Tuesday claimed that Saudi forces had carried out 121 air strikes on Houthi-controlled territory in the preceding days, including a strike on the prison in al-Jawf. The group said they retaliated with attacks on Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as on the Economic City and Khamis Mushait Air Base.

Saudi officials said on Tuesday that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.

Separately on Wednesday, Yemeni government-aligned forces said that they had continued advancing in al-Jawf for a third consecutive day, reaching the vicinity of Bir al-Maraziq and claiming to have severed Houthi supply lines in the area.

The forces also said they had carried out attacks on Houthi positions in Taiz, and that additional reinforcements had been sent on Wednesday to bolster the anti-Houthi National Resistance forces along Yemen’s western coast.

Those claims could not be independently confirmed.

Amid the escalating hostilities, Pakistani officials reiterated this week that any attack on Saudi Arabia could activate the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed last month to strengthen collective deterrence against future attacks.

“If there is unprovoked aggression, or a spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely the Mecca agreement will become operational,” Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told local media.

Iran meanwhile sharply criticised a statement issued earlier this week by Arab League foreign ministers, who condemned what they called “Iranian violations of Yemen’s sovereignty”.

In response, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it “completely rejects the claims regarding Iran’s interference in the affairs of Yemen,” adding that it had “consistently emphasised the need to preserve Yemen’s unity and territorial integrity”. It also said it had supported Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.

articles.title: Zelenskyy's plane was 'almost hit' by a Russian drone over Moldovan airspace, NATO member says
articles.summary: Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was flying from Moldova to Oslo to attend King Harald of Norway's funeral.
articles.body:
NATO member Norway's prime minister said Zelenskyy's plane was "almost hit" by a drone in Moldova.

Moldova, which is to Ukraine's southwest, said a Shahed had entered its airspace on that day.

The drone later crashed in northwestern Moldova, and there are no details yet of how close it got.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's corporate jet was threatened by a drone as he prepared to fly from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister.

"His plane was almost hit by a drone as it took off in Moldova. That's his reality," Jonas Gahr Støre told local broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.

Støre did not provide further details on the incident. Nor did he mention the distance between the drone and Zelenskyy's plane.

The Ukrainian president flew from Moldova on Tuesday evening to attend King Harald of Norway's funeral, before flying to Ottawa to meet with Canadian leaders.

Moldovan authorities said that a drone had entered their country's airspace on Tuesday via the Ukrainian border, adding that preliminary data showed the uncrewed aerial vehicle was a Shahed — Russia's main attack drone . This Shahed entered Moldova twice in the late afternoon, said officials who temporarily closed the country's airspace.

The time of the Shahed's entry, at about 4.20 p.m., matches when Zelenskyy would have been preparing to fly to Oslo.

The Kremlin can launch hundreds of Shaheds and decoy drones at Ukraine in a single day, some of which have been documented wandering into nearby countries, such as Poland and Romania.

NATO has accused Russia of intentionally sending the drones to Eastern Europe to test its reaction to such potential threats. Moscow denies having any such plans.

Moldova's government told Reuters on Wednesday that Zelenskyy's plane was cleared for take-off after the drones exited its airspace.

The Ukrainian president's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.

A separate public statement by officials said the Shahed drone had also initially flown into Romania before returning to Moldovan airspace. It eventually crashed in the northwestern district of Glodeni.

No casualties were reported, though the crash started a fire, officials said.

articles.title: Students in Asia extend lead over a flagging US as AI reshapes education
articles.summary: High-school students across Asia are pulling ahead of their Western peers, an annual global assessment indicates, as artificial intelligence spurs a worldwide race for talent and reshapes how young people learn.
articles.body: High-school students across Asia are pulling ahead of their Western peers, an annual global assessment indicates, as artificial intelligence spurs a worldwide race for talent and reshapes how young people learn. In a troubling trend, reading, science and math performance among 15-year-olds has continued a decline globally across the board, according to the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment released this week by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. But among last year’s top performers were students in the Chinese cities of Beijing and Shanghai, Chinese provinces Jiangsu and Zhejiang, and the city-state of Singapore. Japan and South Korea were also in the Asia-dominated top 10 across all three subjects, along with the semi-autonomous Chinese city of Macao, and the self-governing democracy of Taiwan. Meanwhile, secondary students in the US saw their reading scores fall close to 25-year lows, lagging more starkly behind their counterparts in China, which have long held a lead in the exams known for short as PISA – at least in the four major Chinese jurisdictions that submitted test scores. The exam results come amid an intensifying rivalry between the US and China to outpace the other in technological advancement and direct more funding toward innovation. China has surpassed the US in published scientific reports as well as research spending, on which both nations exceeded $1 trillion in 2024. However, the growing adoption of AI could significantly impact secondary education, the PISA report warned. “Most troubling is the decline in the very skills that matter most in the AI age: evaluating information, making connections across multiple sources, and thinking critically about what we read,” Andreas Schleicher, OECD director for education and skills, wrote in the report. “In a world increasingly flooded with information, our students are less likely to think deeply and separate signal from noise.” China’s data for the PISA tests is not without critics - in part because the test only includes students from the provinces of Shanghai, Beijing, Jiangsu and Zhejiang, some of the country’s wealthiest eastern coastal areas. Nonetheless, the testing has shown continued drop in US scores over the last decade, that have alarmed many educationalists. As technology has progressed, student performance has become less linked with national or family wealth, the latest report said. While it’s difficult to determine the exact correlation between the rise of digital tools and test performance, the study identified one challenge as higher digital distraction in the classroom. Among students from China, Japan and South Korea, fewer than 10% reported that their peers were distracted by digital devices during science lessons, compared with the global average of 28%. As one example of how educators might balance digital tools, the report said Singapore used technology in its classrooms but also emphasized reading comprehension early on. The proportion of “hasty readers,” or students who rushed through their texts and gave incorrect answers, nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025, the report said. As the average performance among OECD countries in science, reading and math has reached record lows, that could have broader economic implications among the world’s biggest nations. The 2025 report cited a Stanford University study that performance meeting a basic level aptitude in PISA among all 15-year-old Americans could add over $40 trillion to the US economy over their working lives. However, the percentage of OECD students below that baseline performance increased last year to 20% from 16% in 2022.

articles.title: North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility, UN’s nuclear watchdog says
articles.summary: North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.
articles.body: North Korea has built a new uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex that could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades, and started operating an expanded annex at its Kangson enrichment site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said. The Vienna-based nuclear watchdog said in a report the findings pointed to a steady expansion of North Korea’s nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations. In the report, dated August 28, the IAEA said it relied on satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by North Korean state media, to track Pyongyang’s nuclear activities. The agency has had no inspectors in North Korea since 2009. It identified a new two-storey building at Yongbyon as the site’s second uranium enrichment facility by comparing state media photographs of a June visit by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un with satellite images taken during the building’s construction. Photographs from the visit indicate gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building, the report said, adding the building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades shown in the photographs. The report also said there were indications that operations began in January at a uranium enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, within an annex that had been constructed in 2024. The IAEA said the developments in North Korea’s nuclear programme violated UN Security Council resolutions. “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of the DPRK’s production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said in a statement to the board of governors on Monday, referring to the North’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. The report accompanied Grossi’s statement. Pyongyang has repeatedly rejected the agency’s authority. North Korea’s mission to the United Nations in Vienna said last September that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapons state had become irreversible and the IAEA had “no legal right … to interfere in the internal affairs of a nuclear weapons state which exists outside the NPT”, referring to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

articles.title: Hong Kong court convicts Wall Street Journal publisher for blocking reporter from union role
articles.summary: A Hong Kong court convicted Dow Jones, the publisher of the Wall Street Journal, on Thursday of attempting to block a former reporter from becoming the head of a press union, but cleared it of unlawfully firing her.
articles.body: A Hong Kong court convicted Dow Jones, the publisher of the Wall Street Journal, on Thursday of attempting to block a former reporter from becoming the head of a press union, but cleared it of unlawfully firing her. Journalist Selina Cheng said she was fired by the Wall Street Journal in July 2024 after refusing demands from senior editors at the paper to sever ties with the Hong Kong Journalists Association and to not advocate for press freedom. Principal Magistrate Cheung Chi-wai David ruled that Dow Jones was guilty of wilfully preventing Cheng from exercising her right, under the city’s Trade Unions Ordinance, to become an officer of a registered trade union in June 2024. “The company required her to obtain permission to run for the chairpersonship of the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) – permission that would have been denied – and asserted that she would not remain employed if she assumed the role,” the magistrate said. Cheng, speaking to reporters following the court hearing, said her case had brought awareness of union suppression in Hong Kong and that employers had no right to have employees consult them before joining a union. “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters,” she said. The company was found not guilty of a second charge that alleged it unlawfully terminated Cheng’s employment contract on July 17, 2024, because she had exercised that right. The magistrate said the possibility that the company dismissed Cheng as part of a genuine corporate restructuring could not be ruled out beyond a reasonable doubt, resulting in an acquittal on the second count. The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 ($12,750). Sentencing is expected at a later date. Dow Jones did not immediately respond to a request for comment following Thursday’s verdict. The company has previously declined to comment on the specifics of Cheng’s allegations. A spokesperson for Dow Jones told Reuters in 2024 the company had made some restructuring decisions but would not comment on specific individuals. Cheng, who covered China’s automobile sector for the Journal in Hong Kong, was elected in 2024 to be the HKJA’s new chairperson at a time of mounting pressure by authorities under a national security crackdown that has seen reporters arrested and pro-democracy media outlets closed. The Wall Street Journal announced changes to its Asia operations in 2024, a move that shifted its “centre of gravity in the region from Hong Kong to Singapore,” it said in a statement at the time. “Consequently, some of our colleagues, mostly in Hong Kong, will be leaving us.” Cheng said at the time that she was told by her supervisor that employees of the Journal should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in a place like Hong Kong given a potential conflict of interest.

articles.title: Primark takes further step into online shopping with home deliveries
articles.summary: The retailer launches the service four years after making its first foray into internet shopping.
articles.body:
Primark has said it plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain, four years after it made its first foray into e-commerce.

The retailer said it had bought a fulfilment facility in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.

Primark did not sell goods online until 2022, when it launched a click-and-collect service which meant shoppers still had to travel to pick up their purchases.

The company said there was "opportunity for profitable growth" through home deliveries, which could help boost trade after Primark reported subdued sales following the recent hot weather.
